screens.title: LINQ: Declarative Queries for Iteration and Strategy
screens.narratorSegment: LINQ, or Language Integrated Query, is a cornerstone of modern C# that allows you to write expressive, declarative queries directly within the language. Think of it as a powerful tool that streamlines operations over various data sources, whether it's collections, databases, or XML. Traditionally, iterating through collections and applying filters or transformations might involve explicit loops and conditional logic, which can become verbose and less flexible. LINQ changes this by providing a rich set of extension methods like Where, Select, Order By, and Group By. This declarative style inherently encapsulates the iteration logic, effectively implementing the Iterator pattern behind the scenes. Moreover, it allows you to easily compose different filtering or projection strategies using lambda expressions, making it a natural fit for the Strategy pattern. For example, instead of writing a custom loop for every filtering scenario, you can simply pass a different lambda expression to a LINQ Where clause, defining a new strategy on the fly. This approach significantly reduces boilerplate code and enhances readability, making your data processing logic much cleaner and more adaptable. LINQ: Declarative Queries for Iteration and Strategy means linq simplifies iterator and strategy patterns by providing declarative, chainable query methods, reducing boilerplate and enhancing flexibility.. In practical terms, simplifying data processing with expressive, chainable operations.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

LINQ: Declarative Queries for Iteration and Strategy

Simplifying data processing with expressive, chainable operations.

Declarative Approach

LINQ allows 'what' to do, not 'how', reducing explicit loops and conditional logic.

Iterator Pattern Simplified

LINQ's methods inherently encapsulate iteration logic, making custom iterators less necessary.

Strategy Pattern Enhanced

Lambda expressions with LINQ methods allow easy composition of different strategies.

Key Takeaway

LINQ transforms data processing by offering a declarative, functional approach that naturally integrates and simplifies Iterator and Strategy patterns.

1

Traditional Iteration

Manual loops and explicit conditions for filtering and transformation.

List<Product> result = new List<Product>();
foreach (var p in products)
{
  if (p.Stock > 100) result.Add(p);
}
2

LINQ Approach

Declarative methods with lambda expressions for concise logic.

products.Where(p => p.Stock > 100);
products.Select(p => p.Name);

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.2›LINQ Example

Practical LINQ: Filtering and Transforming Data

Applying LINQ's `Where` and `Select` for flexible product processing.

Strategy with Lambdas

`Func` acts as a flexible filtering strategy, passed to LINQ's `Where`.

Reduced Boilerplate

Eliminates the need for explicit `foreach` loops and `if` statements for common operations.

Key Takeaway

LINQ enables highly flexible and readable data processing by allowing strategies to be defined as lambda expressions and applied declaratively.

ProductProcessor.cs
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;

public class Product
{
    public string Name { get; set; }
    public decimal Price { get; set; }
    public int Stock { get; set; }
}

public class ProductProcessor
{
    private List<Product> _products;

    public ProductProcessor(List<Product> products)
    {
        _products = products;
    }

    // LINQ approach leveraging Strategy-like behavior
    public IEnumerable<Product> FilterProducts(Func<Product, bool> filterStrategy)
    {
        return _products.Where(filterStrategy);
    }

    public IEnumerable<TResult> TransformProducts<TResult>(Func<Product, TResult> transformStrategy)
    {
        return _products.Select(transformStrategy);
    }

    public static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        var products = new List<Product>
        {
            new Product { Name = "Laptop", Price = 1200, Stock = 50 },
            new Product { Name = "Mouse", Price = 25, Stock = 200 },
            new Product { Name = "Keyboard", Price = 75, Stock = 120 }
        };

        var processor = new ProductProcessor(products);

        Console.WriteLine("Products with stock > 100:");
        foreach (var product in processor.FilterProducts(p => p.Stock > 100))
        {
            Console.WriteLine($"- {product.Name}");
        }

        Console.WriteLine("
Product names and prices:");
        foreach (var item in processor.TransformProducts(p => new { p.Name, p.Price }))
        {
            Console.WriteLine($"- {item.Name} (${item.Price})");
        }
    }
}

screens.title: Async/Await: Modern Asynchronous Programming
screens.narratorSegment: The async and await keywords, introduced in C# 5, were a game-changer for asynchronous programming. Before these keywords, writing non-blocking code often involved complex callback chains, manual thread management, or using constructs like Task. Continue With, which could quickly lead to hard-to-read and maintain spaghetti code. async/await provides a much more readable and maintainable way to handle asynchronous operations, making your code appear almost synchronous while still executing non-blockingly. This significantly impacts how we approach concurrency patterns. While patterns like Producer-Consumer or Reactor are still relevant for highly specific, complex scenarios involving resource contention or message queues, async/await handles the underlying complexity of most input and output-bound asynchronous operations. For example, a Command pattern that previously might have required manual threading for background execution can now simply have an Execute Async open parenthesis close parenthesis method, making the asynchronous nature transparent and easy to implement. The key benefit is that it frees developers from managing low-level threading details, allowing them to focus on the business logic, leading to more responsive and efficient applications. In practical terms, writing non-blocking code with improved readability and maintainability.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6›Chapter 6.2›Async/Await

Async/Await: Modern Asynchronous Programming

Writing non-blocking code with improved readability and maintainability.

Readability & Maintainability

Transforms complex callback chains into sequential-looking, non-blocking code.

Impact on Concurrency Patterns

Simplifies many traditional asynchronous patterns, especially for I/O-bound tasks.

Focus on Business Logic

Developers can concentrate on 'what' to do, not 'how' to manage threads.

Key Takeaway

Async/await fundamentally simplifies asynchronous programming, making non-blocking operations more accessible and reducing the need for complex manual concurrency management.

Old Way

Callbacks & Manual Threads

Complex chains of callbacks or explicit thread management for async tasks.

// Example: Task.ContinueWith
Task.Run(() => LongOperation())
    .ContinueWith(t => UpdateUI(t.Result));
New Way

Async/Await

Sequential-looking code that executes non-blockingly.

// Example: Async Command
public async Task ExecuteAsync()
{
    var result = await LongOperationAsync();
    UpdateUI(result);
}

screens.title: Dependency Injection: The Core of Modern .NET
screens.narratorSegment: Dependency Injection, or DI, is more than just a pattern; it's a core principle and a widely adopted practice in modern. NET applications, especially with frameworks like ASP. NET Core and. NET 5+. At its heart, DI is about inverting control: instead of a class creating its own dependencies, those dependencies are provided to it from an external source, typically a DI container. This approach significantly simplifies the management of dependencies, making your code more modular, testable, and maintainable. The built-in DI container in. NET handles the complex task of creating objects and resolving their dependencies automatically. This means you can focus on defining the contracts, or interfaces, that your services adhere to, and let the container worry about providing the concrete implementations. This externalization of dependency management is crucial for building scalable and flexible applications, as it allows you to easily swap out implementations without modifying the consuming code. It's a powerful tool for achieving loose coupling and promoting a more robust application architecture. In practical terms, leveraging the built-in di container for robust application architecture.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.2›Dependency Injection

Dependency Injection: The Core of Modern .NET

Leveraging the built-in DI container for robust application architecture.

Inversion of Control

Dependencies are provided externally, not created by the consuming class.

Built-in .NET Support

.NET Core/5+ includes a robust DI container for automatic dependency resolution.

Modularity & Testability

Promotes loose coupling, making components easier to test and swap.

Key Takeaway

Dependency Injection is fundamental to modern .NET, providing a powerful mechanism to manage dependencies, enhance modularity, and improve testability.

1

Traditional Dependency

Class creates its own dependencies, leading to tight coupling.

public class MyService
{
    private ILogger _logger;
    public MyService() { _logger = new ConsoleLogger(); }
}
2

DI Managed Dependency

Dependencies are injected, promoting loose coupling and testability.

public class MyService
{
    private ILogger _logger;
    public MyService(ILogger logger) { _logger = logger; }
}

screens.title: Factory Pattern Reimagined with DI
screens.narratorSegment: The Factory pattern is traditionally used to encapsulate object creation logic, allowing a client to create objects without knowing their concrete types. With Dependency Injection, the. NET built-in container can effectively act as your factory, externalizing this creation logic. Instead of manually creating a Concrete Factory and calling its Create open parenthesis close parenthesis method, you register different implementations of an interface with the DI container. Then, you can configure the container to resolve the correct one at runtime, often based on configuration or a factory method you provide. Module 6›Chapter 6.2›DI & Factory

Factory Pattern Reimagined with DI

Using the DI container to dynamically resolve service implementations.

Externalized Creation

DI container manages object creation, replacing explicit factory classes.

Factory Method via Lambda

Register `AddTransient` with a lambda to define dynamic creation logic.

Key Takeaway

DI allows you to implement the Factory pattern declaratively by registering factory methods, making object creation configurable and testable without manual factory classes.

Program.cs
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;
using System;

public interface IMessageSender
{
    void Send(string message);
}

public class EmailSender : IMessageSender
{
    public void Send(string message) => Console.WriteLine($"Emailing: {message}");
}

public class SmsSender : IMessageSender
{
    public void Send(string message) => Console.WriteLine($"SMSing: {message}");
}

public class NotificationService
{
    private readonly IMessageSender _sender;

    public NotificationService(IMessageSender sender)
    {
        _sender = sender;
    }

    public void Notify(string message)
    {
        _sender.Send(message);
    }
}

public class Program
{
    public static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        var serviceCollection = new ServiceCollection();

        // Register IMessageSender with a factory method (Factory pattern via DI)
        serviceCollection.AddTransient<IMessageSender>(provider =>
        {
            bool useEmail = true; // Logic from config or context
            if (useEmail)
            {
                return new EmailSender();
            }
            else
            {
                return new SmsSender();
            }
        });

        serviceCollection.AddTransient<NotificationService>();

        var serviceProvider = serviceCollection.BuildServiceProvider();

        var notificationService = serviceProvider.GetService<NotificationService>();
        notificationService.Notify("Hello from Cohortia!");
    }
}

screens.title: Singleton and Decorator Patterns with DI
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond the Factory pattern, Dependency Injection also offers elegant ways to implement the Singleton and Decorator patterns. The classic Singleton pattern ensures that only one instance of a class exists throughout the application. While you could implement this manually with static properties, the DI container provides a more robust and testable approach. By simply registering a service with Add Singleton, the container guarantees that only a single instance will be created and reused across the application's lifetime. This makes your singletons configurable and easily swappable for testing. For the Decorator pattern, which allows you to add responsibilities to objects dynamically, DI can be used to chain decorators. You register your base service, and then register a decorator that wraps this base service, and so on. The DI container handles the complex construction of this decorated object graph, ensuring that each decorator correctly wraps the previous one. This declarative approach simplifies the setup of complex object compositions, making your code more flexible and easier to extend without modifying existing classes. It's a powerful demonstration of how DI promotes clean architecture and maintainability.

screens.narratorSegment: C# 9 introduced a powerful new feature called records, which are reference types specifically designed for encapsulating data. They come with built-in functionality for immutable properties and value-based equality, making them an excellent fit for implementing Value Objects or simple immutable Data Transfer Objects, often referred to as DTOs. Historically, creating an immutable Value Object in C# required a lot of boilerplate code: you'd need to define properties with only get accessors, write a constructor to initialize them, and crucially, override Equals open parenthesis close parenthesis and Get Hash Code open parenthesis close parenthesis to ensure value-based equality rather than reference equality. Records automate all of this. As you can see in the example, defining an Address as a record is incredibly concise. It automatically provides value equality, a To String open parenthesis close parenthesis implementation, and even with expressions for non-destructive mutation, allowing you to create a new record instance with modified properties without altering the original. This significantly reduces the boilerplate code, making your data structures cleaner, safer, and easier to work with, especially when immutability is a key requirement.

Module 6›Chapter 6.2›Records & Value Objects

C# Records: Concise Value Objects

Simplifying immutable data structures with built-in features.

Immutable Data

Records are ideal for data-centric types with immutable properties.

Value-Based Equality

Automatically provides `Equals()` and `GetHashCode()` for comparing data, not references.

Reduced Boilerplate

Significantly cuts down on code needed for immutable data structures.

Key Takeaway

Records are a modern C# feature that dramatically simplifies the creation and management of immutable Value Objects, improving code conciseness and safety.

RecordExample.cs
using System;

// Traditional immutable Value Object (requires boilerplate)
public class AddressImmutable
{
    public string Street { get; }
    public string City { get; }
    public string ZipCode { get; }

    public AddressImmutable(string street, string city, string zipCode)
    {
        Street = street;
        City = city;
        ZipCode = zipCode;
    }

    // Must override Equals and GetHashCode for value equality
    public override bool Equals(object obj) => obj is AddressImmutable other &&
                                               Street == other.Street &&
                                               City == other.City &&
                                               ZipCode == other.ZipCode;
    public override int GetHashCode() => HashCode.Combine(Street, City, ZipCode);
    public override string ToString() => $"{Street}, {City} {ZipCode}";
}

// Value Object using C# 9 Record (concise)
public record Address(string Street, string City, string ZipCode);

public class RecordExample
{
    public static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        Address address1 = new Address("123 Main St", "Anytown", "12345");
        Address address2 = new Address("123 Main St", "Anytown", "12345");
        Address address3 = new Address("456 Oak Ave", "Otherville", "67890");

        Console.WriteLine($"address1 == address2: {address1 == address2}"); // True (value equality)
        Console.WriteLine($"address1 == address3: {address1 == address3}"); // False

        // With-expressions for non-destructive mutation
        Address address4 = address1 with { City = "Newtown" };
        Console.WriteLine($"Address 4 (modified from 1): {address4}");
    }
}

Beyond the Factory pattern, Dependency Injection also offers elegant ways to implement the Singleton and Decorator patterns. The classic Singleton pattern ensures that only one instance of a class exists throughout the application. While you could implement this manually with static properties, the DI container provides a more robust and testable approach. By simply registering a service with Add Singleton, the container guarantees that only a single instance will be created and reused across the application's lifetime. This makes your singletons configurable and easily swappable for testing. For the Decorator pattern, which allows you to add responsibilities to objects dynamically, DI can be used to chain decorators. You register your base service, and then register a decorator that wraps this base service, and so on. The DI container handles the complex construction of this decorated object graph, ensuring that each decorator correctly wraps the previous one. This declarative approach simplifies the setup of complex object compositions, making your code more flexible and easier to extend without modifying existing classes. It's a powerful demonstration of how DI promotes clean architecture and maintainability.
